locator: Jian ai I (兼愛上), ctext paragraph 4
quote_original: 若使天下兼相愛，愛人若愛其身，猶有不孝者乎？……故視人之室若其室，誰竊？視人身若其身，誰賊？故盜賊亡有。……視人家若其家，誰亂？視人國若其國，誰攻？

quote_translation: Since Aeschylus the poet, having lived sixty-nine years, died at Gela in Sicily, 193 years, Callias the first being archon at Athens.

quote_original: 季孫欲以田賦．使冉有訪諸仲尼．仲尼曰．丘．不識也．三發．卒曰．子為國老．待子而行．若之何子之不言也．仲尼不對．而私於冉有曰．君子之行也．度於禮．施取其厚．事舉其中．斂從其薄．如是則以丘亦足矣．若不度於禮．而貪冒無厭．則雖以田賦．將又不足．且子季孫若欲行而法．則周公之典在．若欲苟而行．又何訪焉．弗聽．
quote_translation: The head of the Ji family wanted to levy the military tax by the field, and sent Ran You to consult Zhongni. Zhongni said: "I know nothing about it." Asked three times, he was finally told: "You are an elder of the state; we are waiting on you before we act. How is it that you will not speak?" Zhongni did not answer, but said privately to Ran You: "The conduct of a gentleman is measured by ritual: in giving he is generous, in undertakings he keeps to the mean, in levies he takes the lightest. By that measure the levy by the qiu is already enough. If he is not measured by ritual and is greedy without limit, then even a levy by the field will not be enough. And if Jisun wants to act by rule, the statutes of the Duke of Zhou are there; if he wants to act as he pleases, why consult me?" He was not heeded.
note: The English is the project's own rendering, hence quote_type 'paraphrase' (conventions §7); this is not a licence dodge — Legge's Zuozhuan (SRC_LEGGE_ZUO) is public domain, but no clean copy of his English was read this session (the Q_036 precedent), so none is quoted. The Chinese is verbatim zh.wikisource.org page 春秋左氏傳/哀公 (revision 7908334, fetched whole via action=raw on 2026-10-04, this session): each segment between ellipses is an exact substring of the page (checked by script), punctuation as the page prints it. source_id and original_source_id are the same row because the edition read is the edition of the licensed original; passages_original_source_distinct warns on that by design (the Q_102 precedent), and leaving original_source_id blank would fail the original-licence guard. 以丘亦足矣 is rendered 'the levy by the qiu is already enough', reading 丘 as the levy unit (as in Lu's 丘甲, E_CN_038, and Zheng's qiu levy, E_CN_007), not as Confucius's personal name, which he uses for himself two clauses earlier (丘．不識也); the pun is in the Chinese and the rendering chooses the fiscal sense. Ran You is Ran Qiu (P_RANQIU). The levy was imposed the next spring (E_CN_041).

locator: 2.3 (wikisource 二之三; Legge Book II, ch. III)
quote_original: 子曰：「道之以政，齊之以刑，民免而無恥；道之以德，齊之以禮，有恥且格。」
quote_translation: The Master said, 'If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. 'If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good.'
note: Chinese verbatim zh.wikisource.org page 論語/爲政第二 (revision 11118094, fetched whole via action=raw on 2026-10-04, this session). locator: 14.17 (wikisource 十四之十七; Legge Book XIV, ch. XVII)
quote_original: 子路曰：「桓公殺公子糾，召忽死之，管仲不死。」曰：「未仁乎？」子曰：「桓公九合諸侯，不以兵車，管仲之力也。如其仁！如其仁！」
quote_translation: Tsze-lu said, 'The Duke Hwan caused his brother Chiu to be killed, when Shao Hu died with his master, but Kwan Chung did not die. May not I say that he was wanting in virtue?' The Master said, 'The Duke Hwan assembled all the princes together, and that not with weapons of war and chariots:-- it was all through the influence of Kwan Chung. Whose beneficence was like his? Whose beneficence was like his?'
note: Chinese verbatim zh.wikisource.org page 論語/憲問第十四 (revision 11118101, fetched whole via action=raw on 2026-10-04, this session). Legge's English verbatim from Project Gutenberg eBook #3330, paragraph numbers and line breaks removed. Kwan Chung is Guan Zhong (P_GUANZHONG); with Q_111 this is what holds his row (L-105(4)). 如其仁 is a crux: Legge reads 'whose beneficence was like his?'; others read 'such was his humaneness'. Either way Confucius judges ren here by public result rather than by personal loyalty, which is why the passage is linked as develops on I_REN at medium reliability.

locator: 14.18 (wikisource 十四之十八; Legge Book XIV, ch. XVIII)
quote_original: 子貢曰：「管仲非仁者與？桓公殺公子糾，不能死，又相之。」子曰：「管仲相桓公，霸諸侯，一匡天下，民到于今受其賜；微管仲，吾其被髮左衽矣！豈若匹夫匹婦之爲諒也，自經於溝瀆，而莫之知也！」
quote_translation: Tsze-kung said, 'Kwan Chung, I apprehend, was wanting in virtue. When the Duke Hwan caused his brother Chiu to be killed, Kwan Chung was not able to die with him. Moreover, he became prime minister to Hwan.' The Master said, 'Kwan Chung acted as prime minister to the Duke Hwan, made him leader of all the princes, and united and rectified the whole kingdom. Down to the present day, the people enjoy the gifts which he conferred. But for Kwan Chung, we should now be wearing our hair unbound, and the lappets of our coats buttoning on the left side. 'Will you require from him the small fidelity of common men and common women, who would commit suicide in a stream or ditch, no one knowing anything about them?'
note: Chinese verbatim zh.wikisource.org page 論語/憲問第十四 (revision 11118101, fetched whole via action=raw on 2026-10-04, this session). Legge's English verbatim from Project Gutenberg eBook #3330, paragraph numbers and line breaks removed; the third opening quotation mark is Legge's own, marking his new paragraph. 一匡天下 ('united and rectified the whole kingdom') is the phrase later writers take up for the unified order; 被髮左衽 marks the non-Zhou peoples, so the claim is that Guan Zhong's order kept the Zhou world from being overrun. With Q_110 this holds P_GUANZHONG (L-105(4)). No idea link: the unification idea belongs to Phase B and is not anchored here.

quote_original: 師曠侍於晉侯．晉侯曰．衛人出其君．不亦甚乎．對曰．或者其君實甚．良君將賞善而刑淫．養民如子．蓋之如天．容之如地．民奉其君．愛之如父母．……若困民之主．匱神乏祀．百姓絕望．社稷無主．將安用之．弗去何為．天生民而立之君．使司牧之．勿使失性．……天之愛民甚矣．豈其使一人肆於民上．以從其淫．而棄天地之性．必不然矣．
quote_translation: Shi Kuang was attending on the marquis of Jin. The marquis said: "The men of Wei have driven out their ruler. Is that not going too far?" He replied: "Perhaps it is their ruler who went too far. A good ruler rewards the good and punishes the vicious; he nurtures the people as his own children, covers them like heaven and holds them like the earth. Then the people serve their ruler and love him as a father and mother. ... But if he brings the people to distress, starves the spirits of their offerings, leaves the hundred clans without hope and the altars of the state without a master, what use is he? What else can be done but remove him? Heaven gave birth to the people and set up rulers over them to shepherd them and not let them lose their nature. ... Heaven's love for the people is very great. Would it let one man run riot above the people, indulging his excesses and abandoning the nature of heaven and earth? Surely not."

locator: Shang xian I (尚賢上第八), 墨子閒詁 卷二
quote_original: 故古者聖王之為政，列德而尚賢，雖在農與工肆之人，有能則舉之，高予之爵，重予之祿，任之以事，斷予之令……故官無常貴，而民無終賤，有能則舉之，無能則下之，舉公義，辟私怨……夫尚賢者，政之本也。
quote_translation: So when the sage kings of old governed, they ranked men by virtue and promoted the worthy. Even someone from the farms or the workshops and market stalls, if he had ability, they raised up: they gave him high rank, a generous salary, responsibility for affairs and the power to give orders. ... So officials were not noble for ever and the common people were not base for ever: the able were raised and the incapable put down, public right was promoted and private grudges set aside. ... Promoting the worthy is the root of government.

quote_original: 宋華元克合晉楚之成。夏。五月。晉士燮會楚公子罷。許偃。癸亥。盟于宋西門之外。曰。凡晉楚無相加戎。好惡同之。同恤菑危。備救凶患。若有害楚。則晉伐之。在晉。楚亦如之。交贄往來。道路無壅。謀其不協。而討不庭。有渝此盟。明神殛之。俾隊其師。無克胙國。
quote_translation: Hua Yuan of Song succeeded in bringing Jin and Chu to terms. In summer, in the fifth month, Shi Xie of Jin met Prince Ba of Chu and Xu Yan, and on the day guihai they swore a covenant outside the west gate of Song, which said: "Jin and Chu shall not make war on each other. They shall share likes and dislikes, take common thought for calamity and danger, and come to each other's rescue in disaster. If anyone harms Chu, Jin shall attack him; and Chu shall do the same for Jin. Envoys and gifts shall go back and forth and the roads shall not be blocked. They shall take counsel together against those who will not keep the peace, and punish those who do not come to court. Whoever breaks this covenant, may the bright spirits destroy him, overthrow his army, and let him not keep his state."

Someone is going to stop it. Even if we say it cannot be done, we must agree; if we refuse, Chu will agree and use it to summon the feudal lords, and we shall lose the leadership of the covenants." The men of Jin agreed.

quote_original: 孟子見梁惠王。王曰：「叟！不遠千里而來，亦將有以利吾國乎？」孟子對曰：「王！何必曰利？亦有仁義而已矣。王曰：『何以利吾國？』大夫曰：『何以利吾家？』士庶人曰：『何以利吾身？』上下交征利而國危矣。……王亦曰仁義而已矣，何必曰利？」
quote_translation: Mencius saw King Hui of Liang. The king said: 'Venerable sir, you have not counted a thousand li too far to come. Surely you have something that will profit my state?' Mencius replied: 'Why must Your Majesty speak of profit? There is humaneness and rightness, and that is all. If the king says "How shall I profit my state?", the great officers say "How shall I profit my house?", and the gentlemen and common people say "How shall I profit myself?", then high and low will fight each other for profit and the state will be in danger. ... Let Your Majesty speak only of humaneness and rightness. Why must you speak of profit?'

quote_original: 孟子見梁襄王。出，語人曰：「望之不似人君，就之而不見所畏焉。卒然問曰：『天下惡乎定？』「吾對曰：『定於一。』「『孰能一之？』「對曰：『不嗜殺人者能一之。』『孰能與之？』「對曰：『天下莫不與也。……如有不嗜殺人者，則天下之民皆引領而望之矣。誠如是也，民歸之，由水之就下，沛然誰能御之？』」
quote_translation: Mencius saw King Xiang of Liang. Coming out, he said to people: 'From a distance he does not look like a ruler; close to, I saw nothing in him to inspire awe. He asked abruptly: "How will the world be settled?" I answered: "It will be settled by unity." "Who can unify it?" I answered: "One who has no taste for killing people can unify it." "Who can give it to him?" I answered: "There is no one in the world who will not give it to him. ... If there were one who had no taste for killing people, the people of the whole world would stretch out their necks to look for him. If that were truly so, the people would turn to him as water flows downward, in a flood that no one could stop."'

quote_original: 孟子曰：「民為貴，社稷次之，君為輕。是故得乎丘民而為天子；得乎天子為諸侯；得乎諸侯為大夫。諸侯危社稷，則變置；犧牲既成，粢盛既潔，祭祀以時，然而旱乾水溢，則變置社稷。」
quote_translation: Mencius said: 'The people are the most important, the altars of the land and grain come next, and the ruler counts least. So whoever wins the common people becomes Son of Heaven, whoever wins the Son of Heaven becomes a lord, whoever wins a lord becomes a great officer. When a lord endangers the altars, he is replaced. When the sacrificial animals are perfect, the grain in the vessels pure and the sacrifices made at the proper seasons, and there is still drought or flood, then the altars themselves are replaced.'

locator: Book of Lord Shang 1, 更法第一 (商君書 卷一)
quote_original: 孝公平畫，公孫鞅、甘龍、杜摯三大夫御於君……公孫鞅曰：「前世不同教，何古之法？帝王不相復，何禮之循？……禮法以時而定，制令各順其宜，兵甲器備各便其用。臣故曰：『治世不一道，便國不必法古。』湯武之王也，不循古而興；殷夏之滅也，不易禮而亡。然則反古者未可必非，循禮者未足多是也。君無疑矣。」
quote_translation: Duke Xiao was deliberating, with three great officers, Gongsun Yang, Gan Long and Du Zhi, in attendance. ... Gongsun Yang said: 'Earlier ages did not teach in the same way, so which antiquity should we copy? The emperors and kings did not repeat one another, so whose rites should we follow? ... Rites and laws were fixed to suit their times; ordinances each followed what was fitting; weapons and equipment each served their use. So I say: there is more than one way to govern an age, and serving the state does not require copying antiquity. Tang and Wu became kings without following antiquity; the Yin and the Xia perished without changing their rites. Those who turn against antiquity are not necessarily wrong, and those who follow the rites deserve no special praise. My lord, have no doubts.'

locator: Book of Lord Shang 17, 賞刑第十七 (商君書 卷四)
quote_original: 聖人之為國也：壹賞，壹刑，壹教。……所謂壹刑者，刑無等級。自卿相將軍以至大夫庶人，有不從王令，犯國禁，亂上制者，罪死不赦。有功於前，有敗於後，不為損刑。有善於前，有過於後，不為虧法。忠臣孝子有過，必以其數斷。
quote_translation: When the sage governs a state, he makes rewards uniform, punishments uniform and teaching uniform. ... What I call uniform punishment is punishment without grades. From chief ministers and generals down to great officers and commoners, whoever disobeys the king's orders, breaks the state's prohibitions or disturbs the ruler's institutions is put to death without pardon. Earlier merit does not lighten the penalty for a later failure; earlier goodness does not bend the law for a later fault. Even a loyal minister or a filial son who does wrong is judged by the full measure.

quote_original: 問者曰：「申不害、公孫鞅，此二家之言孰急於國？」……今申不害言術而公孫鞅爲法。術者，因任而授官，循名而責實，操殺生之柄，課羣臣之能者也。此人主之所執也。法者，憲令著於官府，刑罰必於民心，賞存乎慎法，而罰加乎姦令者也。此臣之所師也。君無術則弊於上，臣無法則亂於下，此不可一無，皆帝王之具也。」……申子言：『治不踰官，雖知弗言。』
quote_translation: Someone asked: 'Shen Buhai and Gongsun Yang: whose teaching is more urgent for a state?' ... 'Now Shen Buhai speaks of technique and Gongsun Yang practises law. Technique means appointing men to office according to their abilities, holding them to the actual duties their titles name, keeping the power of life and death, and examining the abilities of all the officials: this is what the ruler holds in his own hands. Law means statutes and ordinances displayed in the government offices, punishments the people know for certain will follow, rewards for those who keep the law and penalties for those who break orders: this is what the ministers take as their model. Without technique the ruler is blinded above; without law the ministers make disorder below. Neither can be done without; both are the tools of emperors and kings.' ... 'Master Shen says: "In governing, do not go beyond your office; even if you know something, do not speak of it."'

quote_original: 故文王行仁義而王天下，偃王行仁義而喪其國，是仁義用於古不用於今也。故曰：世異則事異。……故明主之國，無書簡之文，以法爲教；無先王之語，以吏爲師；無私劒之捍，以斬首爲勇。
quote_translation: King Wen practised humaneness and rightness and became king of the world; King Yan of Xu practised humaneness and rightness and lost his state. So humaneness and rightness served in antiquity and do not serve today. Hence the saying: when the age is different, its affairs are different. ... So in the state of an enlightened ruler there are no texts written on bamboo: the law is the teaching. There are no sayings of the former kings: the officials are the teachers. There is no valour of private swords: taking enemy heads is courage.

quote_original: 國無常强，無常弱。奉法者强，則國强；奉法者弱，則國弱。……故明主使法擇人，不自舉也；使法量功，不自度也。
quote_translation: No state is always strong or always weak. When those who uphold the law are strong, the state is strong; when those who uphold the law are weak, the state is weak. ... So the enlightened ruler lets the law choose men and does not promote them himself; lets the law measure merit and does not judge it himself.

quote_original: 世之顯學，儒、墨也。儒之所至，孔丘也；墨之所至，墨翟也。……故孔、墨之後，儒分爲八，墨離爲三，取舍相反不同，而皆自謂真孔、墨。孔、墨不可復生，將誰使定世之學乎？……無參驗而必之者，愚也；弗能必而據之者，誣也。故明據先王，必定堯、舜者，非愚則誣也。……儒者破家而葬，服喪三年，大毁扶杖，世主以爲孝而禮之。
quote_translation: The prominent schools of the age are the Ru and the Mohists. The highest of the Ru is Kong Qiu; the highest of the Mohists is Mo Di. ... So after Confucius and Mozi the Ru split into eight and the Mohists into three; what they accept and reject is contrary, yet each calls itself the true Confucius or the true Mozi. Confucius and Mozi cannot come back to life: who is to decide which learning is true? ... To be certain of a thing without checking it against evidence is stupidity; to rely on what one cannot be certain of is deceit. So those who appeal openly to the former kings and claim certainty about Yao and Shun are either stupid or deceitful. ... The Ru ruin their families to pay for burials and mourn for three years, wasting away and leaning on staffs, and the rulers of the age honour them as filial.

quote_original: 昔者吴起教楚悼王以楚國之俗曰：「大臣太重，封君太衆。若此，則上偪主而下虐民，此貧國弱兵之道也。不如使封君之子孫三世而收爵禄，絶減百吏之禄秩，損不急之枝官，以奉選練之士。」悼王行之期年而薨矣，吴起枝解於楚。商君教秦孝公以連什伍，設告坐之過，燔詩書而明法令，塞私門之請而遂公家之勞，禁游宦之民而顯耕戰之士。孝公行之，主以尊安，國以富强，八年而薨，商君車裂於秦。
quote_translation: Long ago Wu Qi advised King Dao of Chu about the customs of Chu: 'The great ministers are too powerful and the enfeoffed lords too many. Like this they press on the ruler above and oppress the people below; this is the way to a poor state and a weak army. It would be better to take back the titles and stipends of the enfeoffed lords' descendants after three generations, reduce the salaries of all the officials, cut away unnecessary offices and use the savings for picked and trained soldiers.' King Dao carried this out for a year and died, and Wu Qi was dismembered in Chu. Lord Shang taught Duke Xiao of Qin to link households in fives and tens and make them liable for failing to denounce crimes, to burn the Odes and Documents and make the laws clear, to block the requests of private houses and reward service to the state, to forbid men to wander in search of office and to honour farmers and soldiers. Duke Xiao carried this out; the ruler was honoured and secure, the state rich and strong; eight years later he died, and Lord Shang was torn apart by chariots in Qin.

quote_original: 馬駭輿，則君子不安輿；庶人駭政，則君子不安位。馬駭輿，則莫若靜之；庶人駭政，則莫若惠之。選賢良，舉篤敬，興孝弟，收孤寡，補貧窮。如是，則庶人安政矣。庶人安政，然後君子安位。傳曰：“君者、舟也，庶人者、水也；水則載舟，水則覆舟。”此之謂也。故君人者，欲安、則莫若平政愛民矣；欲榮、則莫若隆禮敬士矣；欲立功名、則莫若尚賢使能矣。
quote_translation: When the horses shy at the carriage, the gentleman is not safe in the carriage; when the common people shy at the government, the gentleman is not safe in his position. When the horses shy, the best thing is to calm them; when the common people shy at the government, the best thing is to be kind to them. Choose the worthy and good, promote the sincere and respectful, encourage filial piety and brotherly duty, take in orphans and widows, help the poor. Then the common people will be at ease with the government, and only then will the gentleman be safe in his position. A tradition says: 'The ruler is the boat; the common people are the water. The water carries the boat; the water overturns the boat.' This is what it means. So one who rules men, if he wants safety, should govern fairly and love the people; if he wants glory, should honour ritual and respect scholars; if he wants to achieve great things, should promote the worthy and employ the able.

quote_original: 人之性惡，其善者僞也。今人之性，生而有好利焉，順是，故争奪生而辭讓亡焉；……然則從人之性，順人之情，必出於争奪，合於犯分亂理而歸於曓。故必將有師法之化，禮義之道，然後出於辭讓，合於文理，而歸於治。用此觀之，然則人之性惡明矣，其善者僞也。……孟子曰：「今之學者，其性善。」曰：是不然。是不及知人之性，而不察乎人之性、僞之分者也。
quote_translation: Human nature is bad; its goodness is the result of deliberate effort. Human nature is born with a love of profit; follow it, and contention and plunder arise and deference and yielding disappear. ... So to follow human nature and indulge human feelings must lead to contention and plunder, to breaking the bounds of rank and throwing order into chaos, and end in violence. There must therefore be the transforming influence of teachers and laws and the guidance of ritual and rightness; only then do deference and yielding appear, conduct accords with good form and order, and the result is good government. Seen in this light, it is clear that human nature is bad and that its goodness is the result of deliberate effort. ... Mencius says: 'Men learn because their nature is good.' I say: this is not so. It fails to understand human nature and does not see the distinction between nature and deliberate effort.

quote_original: 元年春，王正月。元年者何？君之始年也。春者何？歲之始也。王者孰謂？謂文王也。曷為先言王而後言正月？王正月也。何言乎王正月？大一統也。
quote_translation: 'First year, spring, the king's first month.' What is 'first year'? The first year of the ruler. What is 'spring'? The beginning of the year. Who is 'the king'? King Wen. Why does it put 'king' before 'first month'? Because it is the king's first month. Why speak of 'the king's first month'? To make great the unity of the realm.

quote_original: 九月，戊辰，諸侯盟于葵丘。……夏，會于葵丘，尋盟，且脩好，禮也。……秋，齊侯盟諸侯于葵丘，曰：「凡我同盟之人，既盟之後，言歸于好。」宰孔先歸，遇晉侯曰：「可無會也。齊侯不務德而勤遠略，故北伐山戎，南伐楚，西為此會也。
quote_translation: Ninth month, day wuchen: the lords swore a covenant at Kuiqiu. ... Summer: they met at Kuiqiu to renew the covenant and cultivate good relations, which was in accordance with ritual. ... Autumn: the marquis of Qi swore the lords to a covenant at Kuiqiu, saying: 'All of us who share this covenant, once it is sworn, will return to good relations.' Zai Kong went home first, met the marquis of Jin and said: 'You need not attend the meeting.
